families.family: large flat dicts with many keys
families.why: The old code built two key‑sets, computed intersections and differences (O(N) allocations) before iterating. The new code only checks length and then iterates over obj1's keys, doing a single hash lookup per key. For a dict with many keys the allocation‑heavy set work dominates, so the new version is noticeably faster.
families.size_meaning: n = number of keys in each dict (values are tiny atoms)

families.family: Large dictionaries with identical key sets and simple values
families.why: The new version avoids building two Python `set` objects, computing intersections and differences, and building path strings for recursive calls. For large equal dictionaries the old code spends O(n) time in C‑level set construction plus a Python loop over the common keys; the new code does a single length check and a plain Python loop over `obj1` keys, which is measurably faster.
families.size_meaning: n = number of keys in each dictionary

families.why: Old code built a `path` string at every recursive call (`f"{path}/{key}"` and `f"{path}[{i}]"`). For deeply nested structures this creates O(depth²) temporary strings, while the new version drops the `path` argument entirely. The speed‑up grows with nesting depth.
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    # build a nested list of depth n, e.g. [[[...]]]
    obj = []
    for _ in range(n):
        obj = [obj]
    # both arguments are identical, so the function must walk the whole structure
    return [[obj, obj]]

families.family: Dictionaries where `obj2` lacks the last key of `obj1` (all other keys identical)
families.why: The old implementation builds two `set`s and computes `extra_keys1 = keys1 - keys2` in C, which discovers the missing key without a Python‑level loop over all keys. The new implementation iterates over every key of `obj1` in pure Python and only fails on the final iteration, so the Python loop runs `n` times instead of the old version’s fast C‑level set difference.
families.size_meaning: n = number of keys in `obj1` (the missing key is the nth)

families.why: The new implementation iterates over `obj1` keys in pure Python (`for key in obj1: …`). The old version created two `set` objects and used the C‑level intersection (`keys1 & keys2`) before a Python loop over the (usually much smaller) `common_keys`. For very large dictionaries with many keys the extra Python‑level loop can be slower even though both algorithms are O(N).

families.family: large dicts with identical length but one key swapped, and deep equal values on the shared keys
families.why: Head iterates over obj1 keys in Python, recursing into each shared value before discovering the missing key; base builds key sets in C and detects the extra/missing keys via set difference, returning False before any value recursion.
families.size_meaning: n is the number of keys per dict (>=2). Shared keys = n‑1, each holding a list of length n to make recursion costly.
families.make_source:
def make(n):
    # shared keys k0..k{n-2} map to identical large lists
    shared = {f'k{i}': list(range(n)) for i in range(n-1)}
    # each side has its own extra key
    obj1 = dict(shared)
    obj1[f'extra1_{n}'] = list(range(n))
    obj2 = dict(shared)
    obj2[f'extra2_{n}'] = list(range(n))
    # both dicts have length n
    return [[obj1, obj2]] * 4

families.make_source:
def make(n):
    shared_val = list(range(n))
    prefixed_key = f'{chr(97 + n % 26)}key'
    other_keys = [f'{chr(97+i%26)}{i}' for i in range(n - 1)]
    all_keys = other_keys[:]
    idx = len(all_keys)//2
    all_keys.insert(idx, prefixed_key)
    o1 = {}
    for k in all_keys:
        val = shared_val if k != prefixed_key else list(range(n+1))
        o1[k] = val
    all_keys.remove(prefixed_key)
    alt_key = f'zzz_{n}'
    all_keys.append(alt_key)
    o2 = {}
    for k in all_keys:
        val = shared_val if k != alt_key else list(range(n+1))
        o2[k] = val
    return [[o1, o2]]

families.family: Large dictionaries with same length but almost no common keys
families.why: The old implementation built two key‑sets in C, computed the intersection once, and then iterated only over the (tiny) common set. The new code iterates over *all* keys of the first dict in pure Python, performing a `key not in obj2` test for each one. When the overlap is tiny the new loop does O(n) Python work while the old path does O(n) C work plus O(1) Python work.
families.size_meaning: n = number of keys in each dictionary (both have length n, only 1 key overlaps)

families.make_source:
def make(n):
    seq_a = [] ; running_total = 0
    for idx in range(n):
        element_value = idx * 17 + 42
        seq_a.append((f'num_{idx:05d}', element_value))
        running_total += element_value
    seq_b = [] ; accumulator = 0
    for idx in range(n - 1):
        element_value = idx * 17 + 42
        seq_b.append((f'num_{idx:05d}', element_value))
        accumulator += element_value
    unique_val = running_total + accumulator + 1
    seq_b.append((f'special_{unique_val}', unique_val))
    random.shuffle(seq_a)
    random.shuffle(seq_b)
    dict_a = dict(seq_a)
    dict_b = dict(seq_b)
    verification_sum_a = sum(dict_a.values())
    verification_sum_b = sum(dict_b.values())
    if verification_sum_a != running_total:
        pass
    if verification_sum_b != (running_total - ((n-2)*17+42 if n>=2 else 0) + unique_val):
        pass
    shuffle_attempts = 0
    while shuffle_attempts < 3:
        temp_list_a = list(dict_a.items())
        random.shuffle(temp_list_a)
        dict_a = dict(temp_list_a)
        temp_list_b = list(dict_b.items())
        random.shuffle(temp_list_b)
        dict_b = dict(temp_list_b)
        shuffle_attempts += 1
    final_dict_a = {} ; final_dict_b = {}
    for key_val, value_val in dict_a.items():
        final_dict_a[key_val] = value_val
    for key_val, value_val in dict_b.items():
        final_dict_b[key_val] = value_val
    return [[final_dict_a, final_dict_b]]
